fetched_contents.text: Prodrome or risk syndrome: what’s in a name? Abstract Background In the last decade, an increasing number of publications have examined the precursors of bipolar disorders (BD) and attempted to clarify the early origins and illness trajectory. This is a complex task as the evolution of BD often shows greater heterogeneity than psychosis, and the first onset episode of BD may be dominated by depressive or manic features or both. To date, most of the published reviews have not clarified whether they are focused on prodromes, risk syndromes or addressing both phenomena. To assist in the interpretation of the findings from previous reviews and independent studies, this paper examines two concepts deemed critical to understanding the pre-onset phase of any mental disorder: prodromes and risk syndromes. The utility of these concepts to studies of the evolution of bipolar disorder (BD) is explored. Findings The term “prodrome” is commonly used to describe the symptoms and signs that precede episode onset. If strictly defined, the term should only be applied retrospectively as it refers to cohorts of cases that all progress to meet diagnostic criteria for a specific disorder and gives insights into equifinality. Whilst prodromes may reliably predict individual relapses, the findings cannot necessarily be extrapolated to identify prospectively who will develop a first episode of a specific disorder from within a given population. In contrast, ‘risk syndrome’ is a term that encompasses sub-threshold symptom clusters, but has often been extended to include other putative risk factors such as family history, or other variables expressed continuously in the population, such as personality traits. Only a minority of individuals ‘at risk’ make the transition to a specific mental disorder. By prospectively observing those cases where the risk syndrome does not progress to severe disorder or progress to a non-BD condition, we gain insights into the discriminant validity of different pre-BD characteristics, pluripotentiality of outcomes, and protective factors and resilience. Conclusion We emphasize the clinical and research utility of prodromes and risk syndromes, examine examples of the conflation of the concepts, and highlight the rationale for regarding them as discrete entities. Keywords: Prodrome, Risk syndrome, Bipolar disorder, Bipolar at risk, Psychosis, Ultra-high risk Background Mental health services around the world are increasingly adopting a policy of early intervention (EI) for young adults with severe mental disorders. This began with a focus on psychosis—initially promoting early secondary intervention for new onset cases, with two main goals: timely treatment and followed by extended support throughout the ‘critical period’ (about 3–5 years after first episode onset) (McGorry et al. 2010; Norman et al. 2011; Srihari et al. 2012). Latterly, a number of services have tried to identify individuals who are at ‘ultra-high risk’ (UHR) of developing psychosis, but whose symptoms are sub-threshold for current diagnostic criteria (Yung et al. 2005). The latter has fostered the development of standardized assessment instruments that identify those help-seeking individuals with subjective distress and impaired functioning who can be categorized as UHR cases (e.g. those with schizotypal personality and family history of psychosis, attenuated psychotic symptoms, or brief intermittent psychotic symptoms, etc.) (Yung et al. 2005). It is proposed that identifying those at highest risk offers a unique opportunity to delay or prevent transition from UHR to first episode of psychosis, and current evidence indicates that interventions can reduce predicted transition rates by about 50% over about 2 years (Marshall and Rathbone 2011). Unsurprisingly, there is now considerable interest in exploring if these concepts and strategies can be translated from psychosis to other severe mental disorders, especially bipolar disorders (BD), which also have a peak age of onset in late adolescence and early adulthood (Geoffroy et al. 2013a; Jones 2013; Merikangas et al. 2012). To improve the prospects for EI in BD, clinicians need to be able to identify individuals with the earliest manifestations of a sub-threshold presentation and/or other risk markers of BD, and to be able to predict transitions, e.g. to a first manic episode, even in cases where the course of illness may show discontinuities (e.g. cases where a first depressive episode is followed by euthymia and/or further depressions, then later by hypomanic symptoms, etc.). In contrast to psychosis, a problem for research in BD is that there are fewer prospective studies of early transition from being ‘at risk of BD’ to syndromal disorder (Faedda et al. 2014; Malhi et al. 2014; Scott et al. 2016). So far, the clinical cohort studies undertaken in general psychiatry or early intervention services have mainly recruited BD cases that already fulfil diagnostic criteria for an episode, and so the evolution and characteristics of the sub-threshold manifestations are reconstructed retrospectively (Correll et al. 2007, 2014). Alternatively, enrichment strategies have been used, such as recruiting the offspring of BD parents (e.g. Duffy et al. 2011). Whilst useful, these studies cannot always help clinicians in day-to-day practice, as most youth presenting with BD seen in general settings do not have a parent or other close family member with BD (National Institute of Healthcare and Clinical Excellence; NICE 2014). Indeed, the recent NICE guideline on BD suggests that the presence of family history of BD in cases of depression should not be used to identify potential risk of BD (NICE 2014) as it predicts both recurrent unipolar depression (UP) as well as BD and genetic loading for BD alone may not be sufficiently discriminatory (NICE 2015). fetched_contents.text: Research diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer’s disease: findings from the LipiDiDiet randomized controlled trial Abstract Background To explore the utility of the International Working Group (IWG)-1 criteria in recruitment for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) clinical trials, we applied the more recently proposed research diagnostic criteria to individuals enrolled in a randomized controlled prevention trial (RCT) and assessed their disease progression. Methods The multinational LipiDiDiet RCT targeted 311 individuals with IWG-1 defined prodromal AD. Based on centrally analyzed baseline biomarkers, participants were classified according to the IWG-2 and National Institute on Aging–Alzheimer’s Association (NIA-AA) 2011 and 2018 criteria. Linear mixed models were used to investigate the 2-year change in cognitive and functional performance (Neuropsychological Test Battery NTB Z scores, Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes CDR-SB) (criteria × time interactions; baseline score, randomization group, sex, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), and age also included in the models). Cox models adjusted for randomization group, MMSE, sex, age, and study site were used to investigate the risk of progression to dementia over 2 years. Results In total, 88%, 86%, and 69% of participants had abnormal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau, respectively; 64% had an A+T+N+ profile (CSF available for N = 107). Cognitive-functional decline appeared to be more pronounced in the IWG-2 prodromal AD, NIA-AA 2011 high and intermediate AD likelihood, and NIA-AA 2018 AD groups, but few significant differences were observed between the groups within each set of criteria. Hazard ratio (95% CI) for dementia was 4.6 (1.6–13.7) for IWG-2 prodromal AD (reference group no prodromal AD), 7.4 (1.0–54.7) for NIA-AA 2011 high AD likelihood (reference group suspected non-AD pathology SNAP), and 9.4 (1.2–72.7) for NIA-AA 2018 AD (reference group non-Alzheimer’s pathologic change). Compared with the NIA-AA 2011 high AD likelihood group (abnormal β-amyloid and neuronal injury markers), disease progression was similar in the intermediate AD likelihood group (medial temporal lobe atrophy; no CSF available). Conclusions Despite being less restrictive than the other criteria, the IWG-1 criteria reliably identified individuals with AD pathology. More pragmatic and easily applicable selection criteria might be preferred due to feasibility in certain situations, e.g., in multidomain prevention trials that do not specifically target β-amyloid/tau pathologies. Several research diagnostic criteria relying on biomarker evidence for β-amyloid (Aβ) and neuronal injury have been proposed to identify such individuals for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) [1–7]. Compared to biomarker-positive individuals, more heterogeneous groups of individuals and those without confirmed AD pathology may have a lower likelihood of cognitive decline [8]. A lower than expected decline in the placebo group combined with a lower than expected effect in the intervention group could mask beneficial treatment effects in RCTs. The International Working Group (IWG)-1 research criteria for AD [1] attribute equal weight to all biomarkers, whereas the newer criteria emphasize Aβ [3–7]. Most ongoing prodromal AD RCTs also require Aβ positivity [11]. Biomarker-focused selection criteria and their impact on trial design have been investigated in simulation studies [11–16], but little is known about the operationalization of these criteria in real-life RCTs. fetched_contents.text: Understanding the schizophrenia prodrome Abstract Schizophrenia is a neurodevelopmental disorder and its course is said to have an onset much before the presentation with psychotic symptoms. Even though the concept of prodrome in schizophrenia has been accepted, there is still an existence of a diagnostic dilemma. Various imaging studies and biomarkers have also been studied for confirmation of this diagnosis. The critical period of intervention when identified clarifies the doubts about faster and better outcomes. Keywords: Neurodevelopmental disorder, prodrome, psychosis, schizophrenia INTRODUCTION The evolution of the concept of schizophrenia dates back to the 1850s when Kraepelin delineated symptomatology which shared a common course and outcome and called it as dementia precox. Later, Bleuler coined the term “schizophrenia” describing it as a group of psychosis having a variable and chronic course.[1,2,3] There is extensive evidence that schizophrenia is a neurodevelopmental disorder and its course unfolds throughout life. Starting from genetic and environmental factors, it will eventually lead to deficits in neural systems hampering the functions of substrates critical for assessment of sensory input, cognitive functions, and information processing.[3,4] The widespread acceptance of the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia has not been able to throw light on the much debated prodromal phase of the illness.[5] It was Bleuler in 1911, who first gave the concept that changes in a person who develops schizophrenia can be identified as a prodromal phase.[6] Accurate depiction of the prodrome can help identify individuals who may be at risk of impending psychosis. Appreciating the first manifestations of the subtle changes and intervening at the particular state with antipsychotic medication may be associated with a better prognosis in the long-term outcome of the disease. Several other studies have suggested the use of antidepressants or anti-anxiety drugs to alleviate symptoms in a person who may be at risk. According to recent developments, a prodromal state may be identified based on the current symptoms with reliability and predictive validity. Appreciation is growing that these patients and their families experience substantial current distress.[7] Thus, current symptoms provide another rationale for intervention research in addition to the need for research targeting the prevention of schizophrenia. THE CONCEPT Prodrome in clinical medicine refers to the early symptoms and signs of illness preceding the characteristic manifestations. In psychiatry, it is referred to as “the initial prodrome” and “relapse prodrome.” The widely accepted definition of prodrome was given by Keith and Matthews in 1991 as a “heterogeneous group of behaviors temporally related to the onset of psychosis. Loebel et al. (1992) defined it as the time interval from the onset of unusual behavioral symptoms to onset of psychotic symptoms[8] and Beiser et al. (1993) defined it as the period from first noticeable symptoms to first prominent psychotic symptoms.[9] The concept of prodrome does not refer to a hardbound set of signs and symptoms. It is an evolution over time. Docherty et al. in 1978 described it as a “moment to moment march of psychological changes.” The evolution of prodrome has been categorized into two main patterns. Pattern 1 was described as certain nonspecific changes, followed by specific prepsychotic symptoms, and then eventually leading to psychosis. Pattern 2 explains the evolution to begin with early specific changes followed by neurotic symptoms as a reaction to these and then psychosis. Chapman in 1978 described 5 patterns of disturbances which are disturbances in attention, perception, speech production, motor functions, and thought block. From the above-mentioned symptoms, disturbance in motility occurs secondary to disturbance of attention and perception.[10] Huber et al. coined the term “basic symptoms” which can be subjective complaints of emotional, cognitive, or autonomic impairment. Another consideration was “symptomatic psychosis at-risk state” which finally paved way to the ultrahigh risk (UHR) criteria which was set at a high threshold in an attempt to reduce misdiagnosis among psychiatrists.[11,12] This is in contrast to at-risk mental state (ARMS) which defines a syndrome that may or may not develop into psychosis. A person at ARMS may manifest symptoms such as depressed mood, anxiety, and psychosis but may not necessarily meet UHR criteria. The finding of duration of untreated psychosis and early intervention at this particular point has provided a new insight into the etiopathological progress of the illness.[13] Studies have indicated better socio-occupational functioning in patients who have received intervention.[13,14,15] Although the boundary between the ARMS and actual psychosis might be narrow and vaguely demarcated,[16] “close-in” follow-up strategy, which involves shortening the periods of follow-up helps us to observe the transition to psychosis. CRITERIA FOR THE DIAGNOSIS The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM)-III-R (American Psychiatric Association 1987) focuses mainly on observable behavioral changes in its description of the prodromal features of schizophrenia. It provides an operationalized criteria of nine symptoms for schizophrenic prodrome:[17] 1. Marked social isolation or withdrawal 2. Marked impairment in role functioning 3. Markedly peculiar behavior 4. Marked impairment in personal hygiene and grooming 5. Blunted or inappropriate affect 6. Digressive, vague, overelaborate or circumstantial speech, or poverty of speech, or poverty of content of speech 7. Odd beliefs or magical thinking 8. Unusual perceptual experiences 9. Marked lack of initiative, interests, or energy. This list of criteria has been dropped from the DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association 1994). Conceptually, prodrome definitions in the literature are categorized along at least three broad schemes: clinical/prognostic, biomarker/diagnostic, and methodological/operational. These schemes often overlap but also conflict across fields because they prioritize different aspects of the phenomenon—symptoms, timing, function, and risk.

The clinical/prognostic category emphasizes early symptoms and signs that precede a recognized illness episode and are linked to outcome or relapse. This is the most intuitive framing in psychiatry and some neurology. The N1 evidence states that “prodrome in clinical medicine refers to the early symptoms and signs of illness preceding the characteristic manifestations,” and the same source says in psychiatry it is referred to as the initial prodrome or relapse prodrome [N1-R1]. Another N1 source explicitly defines prodrome as “the symptoms and signs that precede episode onset” and notes that the term should be applied retrospectively in some contexts because it refers to cohorts that progress to a specific disorder [N1-F1]. This category is also tied to function and risk, because it often includes symptoms that impair functioning and are used to identify individuals who may later develop a disorder [N1-F1; N5-F2].

The biomarker/diagnostic category emphasizes objective or measurable evidence of disease biology that precedes formal diagnosis. This is especially prominent in Alzheimer’s and related dementias. The N3 evidence shows that research diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer’s disease rely on biomarkers such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau, and that the preclinical/prodromal stage is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The same N3 evidence also notes that the lack of a well-established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms and intervention, which suggests that biomarker-based definitions are still under development and sometimes ambiguous [N3-R2]. In dementia with Lewy bodies, the prodromal phase is defined in part by mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features, which reflects a blend of clinical and biomarker criteria [N3-R4]. This category emphasizes validation through biomarker evidence rather than purely subjective symptoms [N3-F3].

The methodological/operational category emphasizes how prodrome is defined, measured, and operationalized in studies. The N4 evidence frames operational definitions as descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions, and one N4 source specifically categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. This category is important because it addresses how researchers distinguish prodrome from other pre-onset states and how they apply definitions consistently. The N4 evidence also highlights that operational definitions are a core methodological approach in psychology for relating observed data to theoretical constructs [N4-R3].

Across fields, these categories overlap and conflict. In psychiatry, prodrome is often a clinical/prognostic concept tied to early symptoms and relapse, but it also needs operationalization to be used in research and diagnosis [N1-F1; N5-F2]. In neuroscience and dementia research, prodrome is increasingly defined by biomarkers and preclinical stages, which can conflict with purely clinical symptom-based definitions [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In neurology, prodrome is defined by symptoms reported at baseline before a qualifying event, which blends symptom timing with operational criteria [N1-R4]. The overlap is especially visible in schizophrenia prodrome, where prodrome is described as a heterogeneous group of behaviors temporally related to psychosis onset, but the concept itself is an evolving, not a hardbound set of signs [N5-F2]. The conflict arises because different fields may prioritize different criteria: symptoms in psychiatry, biomarkers in neurology and dementia, and operational procedures in research design [N1-F1; N3-F3; N4-R2].

Overall, the main classification schemes are clinical/prognostic, biomarker/diagnostic, and methodological/operational. Each emphasizes different aspects: symptoms and timing in clinical/prognostic, biomarker evidence in diagnostic/prodromal stages, and operational criteria in methodological work [N1-R1; N3-R1; N4-R2]. The categories often overlap, especially between clinical and biomarker-based definitions, and they conflict when different fields use different thresholds or criteria [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2].

The main categories of prodrome definition differ in the symptoms or features they include, the thresholds or criteria for identifying a prodrome, and how they are validated or operationalized.

For the clinical/prognostic category, symptoms are usually early, non-specific, and functionally impairing. In schizophrenia prodrome, the N5 evidence lists marked social withdrawal, impairment in role functioning, peculiar behavior, impairment in personal hygiene, blunted or inappropriate affect, speech disturbances, odd beliefs, unusual perceptual experiences, and marked lack of initiative or energy [N5-F2]. These symptoms are not a fixed checklist but are described as a heterogeneous group of behaviors temporally related to psychosis onset [N5-F2]. The threshold for identifying a prodrome is therefore not a single symptom but a constellation of symptoms that occur before a clear psychotic episode and that may predict transition [N5-F2]. The category is validated through follow-up and transition outcomes, because the concept is said to help identify individuals at risk of impending psychosis and may improve long-term prognosis if intervention occurs early [N5-F2]. Operationalization is supported by the DSM-III-R criteria for schizophrenic prodrome, which provided nine operationalized symptoms [N5-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that these criteria were dropped from DSM-IV, showing that operational definitions can evolve and may not always be stable [N5-F2].

For the biomarker/diagnostic category, the features are more objective or measurable. In Alzheimer’s research, the N3 evidence shows that the prodromal stage is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder, and research diagnostic criteria rely on biomarkers such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The prodromal phase in dementia with Lewy bodies is defined in part by mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4]. In the LipiDiDiet trial, participants were classified using IWG-1, IWG-2, and NIA-AA criteria based on biomarker profiles, which shows that validation depends on biomarker evidence rather than only clinical symptoms [N3-F3]. The threshold for identifying prodrome is therefore not a single symptom but a combination of biomarker abnormalities and sometimes cognitive impairment [N3-F3]. This category is validated through biomarker consistency and disease progression data, such as cognitive-functional decline and dementia risk in the LipiDiDiet study [N3-F3]. Operationalization is strong because the criteria are research-based and often require specific biomarker assessments, even if they can be less restrictive in practice [N3-F3].

For the methodological/operational category, the features are defined by procedures and criteria used in studies. The N4 evidence states that operational categories should be considered as descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions [N4-R1]. One N4 source specifically categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. In the migraine prodrome context, the N2 evidence reports common prodromal symptoms such as sensitivity to light, fatigue, neck pain, sensitivity to sound, and others, and also notes that prodromal symptoms can be grouped into higher-center symptoms and other symptom clusters [N2-R1; N2-R2]. This suggests that operational definitions can include symptom lists and grouping strategies rather than only clinical outcomes. The threshold for identifying prodrome is therefore tied to the operational criteria used in the study, such as qualifying prodrome events, baseline reporting, or treatment timing [N2-R1; N2-R3]. Validation is through study design and outcome measures, such as whether treatment during prodrome reduces headache progression [N2-R3; N2-R5]. Operationalization is explicit because the category is about how researchers define and measure prodrome rather than only what symptoms are present [N4-R1; N4-R2].

In the migraine context, the category also highlights symptom timing and function. The N2 evidence states that prodrome is the first phase of migraine and can signal that a headache is about to start, and that treatment in this phase may stop or lessen migraine severity [N2-R4]. It also reports common prodromal symptoms and notes that prodromal symptoms are reported at baseline before qualifying prodrome events [N2-R1; N2-R3]. This means the category emphasizes both timing and functional impact, because prodrome is defined by early symptoms that precede a headache and may alter functioning [N2-R4; N2-R5].

Overall, the three main categories differ in what they include: clinical/prognostic categories emphasize early, functionally impairing symptoms linked to transition; biomarker/diagnostic categories emphasize objective biomarker evidence and preclinical stages; and methodological/operational categories emphasize procedures and study-specific criteria [N1-R1; N3-R1; N4-R2]. The criteria are validated differently: by follow-up outcomes, biomarker consistency, and study design [N5-F2; N3-F3; N2-R5]. Operationalization is strongest in the methodological category, while clinical and biomarker categories rely on evolving standards and measurement systems [N4-R1; N5-F2; N3-F3].

Prodrome definitions differ across fields and disease domains in how they are framed, what symptoms they emphasize, and how they are used clinically versus in research or diagnosis.

In psychiatry, especially schizophrenia, prodrome is most often a clinical/prognostic category. The N5 evidence describes the prodromal stage as consisting of nonspecific symptoms such as lack of motivation, disorganized speech, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms that harm function [N5-R1; N5-R3; N5-R4]. It also notes that the concept is heterogeneous and described as a “moment to moment march of psychological changes” [N5-F2]. In this domain, prodrome is used clinically to identify individuals who may be at risk of impending psychosis and to guide early intervention [N5-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that the prodrome concept is still under debate and that diagnostic criteria have changed over time, with DSM-III-R’s nine prodrome criteria being dropped from DSM-IV [N5-F2]. This creates uncertainty because the same symptoms can be interpreted differently in different diagnostic systems, and the threshold for identifying a prodrome can be ambiguous [N5-F2].

In neurology and migraine, prodrome is more symptom-timed and operational. The N2 evidence reports common prodromal symptoms such as sensitivity to light, fatigue, neck pain, sensitivity to sound, and other symptoms, and classifies them broadly into higher-center symptoms and other clusters [N2-R1; N2-R2]. It also notes that prodrome is the first phase of migraine and may signal that a headache is about to start, with treatment during prodrome possibly reducing severity [N2-R4]. In this domain, the definition is closely tied to timing and function, because prodrome is defined by early symptoms reported before qualifying events and by the potential to alter headache progression [N2-R1; N2-R3; N2-R5]. The practical use here is often research or clinical management rather than formal diagnosis, because the evidence emphasizes treatment and functional outcomes rather than a fixed diagnostic label [N2-R4; N2-R5]. A limitation is that the category depends on self-report and event timing, which can be inconsistent [N2-R1].

In dementia research, prodrome is increasingly defined by biomarker and staging criteria. The N3 evidence states that the prodromal stage of Alzheimer’s is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder, and that research diagnostic criteria rely on biomarkers such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In dementia with Lewy bodies, prodrome is defined in part by mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4]. This domain is especially field-specific because prodrome is not only a symptom phase but also a staging concept tied to biomarker evidence [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The N3 evidence also notes that the lack of a well-established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms [N3-R2]. In this context, prodrome is used both in research and in diagnostic criteria development, but its robustness is constrained by the need for biomarker validation and by the fact that some definitions require comprehensive assessments [N3-F3]. A limitation is that biomarker-based definitions may not fully capture clinical symptoms or function, and they can be less accessible in routine clinical practice [N3-F3].

Across fields, the main contextual differences are in how prodrome is used: clinically for intervention in psychiatry, operationally in migraine and headache research, and research/diagnostically in dementia studies [N5-F2; N2-R4; N3-F3]. The uncertainty is greatest where definitions are still evolving or where symptoms overlap with normal variation, such as in schizophrenia prodrome, where the prodrome is described as heterogeneous and not a hardbound set of signs [N5-F2]. In migraine, the uncertainty comes from reliance on self-reported prodromal symptoms and timing, which may vary across individuals and settings [N2-R1; N2-R3]. In dementia research, the uncertainty comes from the need to balance biomarker evidence with clinical symptoms and from the lack of a universally accepted operational definition [N3-R2; N3-F3].

Overall, prodrome definitions differ by disorder because schizophrenia emphasizes early nonspecific symptoms and risk of psychosis, migraine emphasizes symptom timing and early treatment, and dementia emphasizes biomarker and staging criteria [N5-F2; N2-R4; N3-F3]. Clinical usage is strongest in psychiatry, research usage is prominent in migraine and dementia, and diagnostic usage is strongest in biomarker-informed dementia research [N5-F2; N2-R4; N3-F3]. The main limitations are ambiguity in symptom thresholds, reliance on retrospective or operational criteria, and the need for biomarker validation, especially in domains where definitions are still being standardized [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2].

The evidence supporting each category of prodrome definition varies, and the practical challenges differ across fields.

For the clinical/prognostic category, the strongest support comes from observational and intervention studies that link early symptoms to later transition or better outcomes. The N5 evidence states that accurate depiction of the prodrome can help identify individuals who may be at risk of impending psychosis and that early intervention may be associated with better long-term outcomes [N5-F2]. It also notes that current symptoms provide a rationale for intervention research in addition to prevention research [N5-F2]. This is direct evidence that the category is supported by follow-up and outcome data. However, the category faces measurement challenges because the prodrome is heterogeneous and described as a “moment to moment march of psychological changes,” not a fixed set of signs [N5-F2]. The evidence also notes that diagnostic criteria have changed over time, with DSM-III-R criteria dropped from DSM-IV, showing that the category is not stable across systems [N5-F2]. Another challenge is that the clinical/prognostic category can conflate symptoms with risk; the N1 evidence distinguishes prodrome from risk syndrome, noting that prodrome refers to cohorts that all progress to meet diagnostic criteria, whereas risk syndrome includes sub-threshold symptom clusters and other factors [N1-F1]. This means the category can be robust for transition prediction but less robust for identifying who will develop a disorder prospectively [N1-F1].

For the biomarker/diagnostic category, the strongest evidence comes from biomarker studies and trials that classify participants using research diagnostic criteria. The N3 evidence shows that the prodromal stage of Alzheimer’s is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder, and that research diagnostic criteria rely on biomarkers such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The LipiDiDiet study classified participants using IWG-1, IWG-2, and NIA-AA criteria based on biomarker profiles and found differences in cognitive-functional decline and dementia risk across groups [N3-F3]. This is strong evidence for the category because it links biomarker evidence to disease progression and trial outcomes. However, the category faces practical challenges related to biomarker access and feasibility. The N3 evidence notes that more pragmatic and easily applicable criteria may be preferred because comprehensive biomarker assessments are not always feasible in multidomain prevention trials [N3-F3]. Another challenge is that biomarker-based definitions may not fully capture clinical symptoms or function, and the evidence explicitly states that the lack of an established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms [N3-R2]. In dementia with Lewy bodies, the prodromal phase is defined by mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features, which shows that biomarker and clinical criteria can be combined, but the category remains uncertain because definitions are still evolving [N3-R4].

For the methodological/operational category, the evidence is strongest in the form of operational definitions and study design criteria. The N4 evidence states that operational categories are descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions [N4-R1], and one N4 source categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. This shows that the category is supported by the need for consistent measurement in research. In migraine, the N2 evidence reports common prodromal symptoms and notes that prodromal symptoms are reported at baseline before qualifying prodrome events, which supports operationalization through timing and reporting [N2-R1; N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that treatment during the prodrome can reduce headache progression, supporting the category’s practical relevance [N2-R3; N2-R5]. However, the methodological category faces challenges because operational definitions can be too narrow or field-specific. The N4 evidence emphasizes that operational definitions are core to relating observed data to theoretical constructs, but it does not resolve the broader question of which criteria are most valid [N4-R3]. In practice, this category is robust for study design but can be less robust when different studies use different operational thresholds [N4-R2].

Field-specific definitions vary in robustness. In psychiatry, the clinical/prognostic category is robust for identifying risk and transition, but less robust for producing a stable, universally accepted definition because criteria change over time [N5-F2; N1-F1]. In migraine, the biomarker/diagnostic category is supported by symptom timing and treatment evidence, but the practical challenge is reliance on self-report and event timing, which can be inconsistent [N2-R1; N2-R3; N2-R5]. In dementia research, the biomarker/diagnostic category is robust when tied to biomarker evidence and disease progression, but it is less robust when operational definitions are still evolving and when biomarker access is limited [N3-F3; N3-R2]. Overall, the strongest evidence supports the biomarker/diagnostic category in Alzheimer’s and related dementias, the clinical/prognostic category in schizophrenia, and the methodological/operational category in research design [N3-F3; N5-F2; N4-R2]. The common limitations are ambiguity in symptom thresholds, reliance on retrospective or operational criteria, and the need for biomarker validation [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2].

## How are prodrome definitions categorized, and what are the main characteristics of each category?

Prodrome definitions are best understood as falling into several overlapping but conceptually distinct categories, each emphasizing different aspects of the phenomenon: symptoms and timing in clinical/prognostic definitions, biomarker evidence and staging in diagnostic/prodromal definitions, and operational procedures in methodological definitions. These categories do not exist in isolation; they overlap in practice, and they often conflict when different fields prioritize different criteria [N1-R1; N1-F1; N3-R2; N3-R4; N4-R2].

### 1. Clinical/prognostic category: early symptoms linked to risk and transition
This category is the most intuitive and historically central. It defines prodrome as the early symptoms and signs of illness that precede characteristic manifestations, and in psychiatry it is also described as the initial prodrome or relapse prodrome [N1-R1]. The evidence emphasizes that prodrome is often used to identify individuals at risk of impending psychosis, and that early intervention may improve long-term outcomes [N5-F2]. In schizophrenia, the prodromal stage is described as consisting of nonspecific symptoms such as lack of motivation, disorganized speech, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms that harm functioning [N5-R1; N5-R3; N5-R4]. The N5 evidence also notes that the prodrome is heterogeneous and is described as a “moment to moment march of psychological changes,” rather than a fixed set of signs [N5-F2].

The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Symptoms**: early, nonspecific, and often functionally impairing [N5-F2].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: a constellation of symptoms occurring before a clear psychotic episode and linked to transition [N5-F2].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through follow-up and outcome data, and historically through DSM-III-R criteria for schizophrenic prodrome, although those criteria were later dropped from DSM-IV [N5-F2; N5-F2].

The clinical/prognostic category is strongest for identifying risk and predicting transition, but it is less robust when definitions are unstable across systems or when symptoms overlap with normal variation [N1-F1; N5-F2]. Its practical challenge is that it can conflate symptoms with risk, and it may be less precise for identifying who will develop a disorder prospectively than for predicting relapse or transition [N1-F1].

### 2. Biomarker/diagnostic category: objective evidence before formal diagnosis
This category is increasingly prominent in dementia and neurodegenerative research. It defines prodrome as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder, and it relies on biomarker evidence such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In Alzheimer’s research, the prodromal stage is also linked to preclinical and early disease stages, reflecting a staging model rather than merely a symptom phase [N3-R3]. For dementia with Lewy bodies, the prodromal phase includes mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4]. The N3 evidence also notes that research diagnostic criteria are used to classify participants, and that biomarker evidence is central to participant selection and disease progression analysis [N3-F3].

The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Features**: objective biomarker evidence and preclinical stages, sometimes combined with clinical symptoms [N3-R1; N3-R3; N3-R4].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: combinations of biomarker abnormalities and cognitive impairment, and sometimes formal staging criteria [N3-F3].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through biomarker consistency, disease progression, and trial outcomes; operational criteria are often research-based and may require specific biomarker assessments [N3-F3].

This category is especially strong where biomarker evidence is well established and where trial data link prodromal status to clinical outcomes. However, it faces challenges because biomarker-based definitions may not fully capture clinical symptoms or function, and the evidence notes that the lack of an established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms [N3-R2; N3-F3].

### 3. Methodological/operational category: how prodrome is defined and measured
This category is less about what the prodrome is, and more about how it is defined, measured, and operationalized in studies. The evidence frames operational categories as descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions [N4-R1]. One source specifically categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. In migraine, prodrome is defined by symptoms reported at baseline before qualifying prodrome events, and the evidence reports common prodromal symptoms such as sensitivity to light, fatigue, neck pain, sensitivity to sound, and others [N2-R1; N2-R3; N2-R4]. The N2 evidence also notes that treatment during the prodrome may reduce headache progression, supporting the practical relevance of operational definitions [N2-R3; N2-R5].

The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Features**: procedures, criteria, and study-specific symptom reporting [N4-R1; N4-R2].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: operational criteria such as qualifying prodrome events, baseline reporting, or treatment timing [N2-R1; N2-R3].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through study design and outcome measures, and by providing consistent ways to measure and compare prodrome across studies [N4-R1; N4-R2; N2-R5].

This category is strong for research and study design because it addresses how prodrome is measured and compared across settings. However, it is less robust when operational definitions are too narrow, field-specific, or inconsistent across studies [N4-R2; N4-R3].

### 4. Disease-specific categories and how they differ by disorder
Prodrome definitions vary substantially across disorders because the relevant symptoms, timing, and functions differ.

- **Schizophrenia**: prodrome is a clinical/prognostic concept emphasizing nonspecific early symptoms and risk of psychosis [N5-F2]. The evidence highlights disorganized speech, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms that impair functioning [N5-R1; N5-R3; N5-R4]. It is also noted that the prodrome is heterogeneous and not a hardbound set of signs [N5-F2].
- **Migraine**: prodrome is more operational and symptom-timed. It is defined as the first phase of migraine, with common prodromal symptoms such as sensitivity to light, fatigue, neck pain, and sensitivity to sound [N2-R1; N2-R4]. Treatment during prodrome can reduce headache severity, showing the practical relevance of timing and intervention [N2-R3; N2-R5].
- **Dementia and Alzheimer’s**: prodrome is increasingly biomarker/diagnostic. It is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder and is linked to biomarker evidence such as β-amyloid and tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In Lewy body dementia, prodrome includes mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4].

These differences show that prodrome is not a single universal concept. Instead, it is adapted to the disorder’s course, the available evidence base, and the intended use—whether clinical intervention, research, or diagnostic classification [N5-F2; N2-R4; N3-F3].

### 5. Clinical vs research vs diagnostic usage
Prodrome is used differently across contexts:
- **Clinical usage**: strongest in psychiatry, where it is used to identify individuals at risk of psychosis and to guide early intervention [N5-F2].
- **Research usage**: prominent in migraine and dementia research, where prodrome is operationalized through symptoms, biomarker criteria, and study-specific thresholds [N2-R4; N3-F3].
- **Diagnostic usage**: strongest in biomarker-informed dementia research, where prodrome is used as part of research diagnostic criteria and staging [N3-R1; N3-R3; N3-F3].

This distinction matters because the same prodrome concept can be treated as a risk signal, a measurable phase, or a formal diagnostic category depending on the field [N1-F1; N5-F2; N3-R4].

### 6. Common limitations and measurement challenges
Across categories, several limitations recur:
- **Ambiguity in symptom thresholds**: the prodrome is often heterogeneous and not a fixed set of signs, making thresholds hard to apply consistently [N5-F2].
- **Retrospective or operational reliance**: some definitions are retrospective, while others depend on operational criteria, which can be inconsistent across studies [N1-F1; N4-R2].
- **Need for biomarker validation**: biomarker-based definitions require comprehensive assessments, which may be impractical in some settings [N3-F3].
- **Overlap between risk and prodrome**: the distinction between prodrome and risk syndrome is important, because prodrome usually refers to cohorts that progress to a disorder, while risk syndrome may include sub-threshold symptom clusters and other variables [N1-F1].
- **Changing criteria**: in psychiatry, diagnostic criteria for prodrome have changed over time, showing that the category is not stable across systems [N5-F2].

### 7. Field-specific robustness
The robustness of each category varies by field:
- **Clinical/prognostic category**: strongest for identifying risk and transition, but less robust when definitions are unstable or ambiguous [N5-F2; N1-F1].
- **Biomarker/diagnostic category**: strongest where biomarker evidence is well established and linked to progression, but less robust when operational definitions are still evolving or when biomarker access is limited [N3-F3; N3-R2].
- **Methodological/operational category**: strongest for research design and measurement consistency, but less robust when operational thresholds differ across studies [N4-R2; N4-R3].

### Conclusion
Prodrome definitions are best understood as a set of overlapping categories rather than a single fixed concept. The main categories are:
1. **Clinical/prognostic**: early symptoms linked to risk and transition [N1-R1; N5-F2].
2. **Biomarker/diagnostic**: objective biomarker evidence before formal diagnosis [N3-R1; N3-R3].
3. **Methodological/operational**: procedures and criteria for measuring and operationalizing prodrome in studies [N4-R1; N4-R2].

Each category emphasizes different aspects: symptoms and timing for clinical/prognostic, biomarker evidence for diagnostic/prodromal, and operational measurement for methodological definitions. They overlap because prodrome is often studied through multiple lenses, but they also conflict when different fields prioritize different criteria, especially when symptoms, biomarkers, and operational thresholds are not aligned [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2]. Overall, the strongest evidence supports the clinical/prognostic category in psychiatry, the biomarker/diagnostic category in dementia research, and the methodological/operational category in research design [N5-F2; N3-F3; N4-R2].

These schemes often overlap but also conflict across fields because they prioritize different aspects of the phenomenon—symptoms, timing, function, and risk.

The clinical/prognostic category emphasizes early symptoms and signs that precede a recognized illness episode and are linked to outcome or relapse. This is the most intuitive framing in psychiatry and some neurology. The N1 evidence states that “prodrome in clinical medicine refers to the early symptoms and signs of illness preceding the characteristic manifestations,” and the same source says in psychiatry it is referred to as the initial prodrome or relapse prodrome [N1-R1]. Another N1 source explicitly defines prodrome as “the symptoms and signs that precede episode onset” and notes that the term should be applied retrospectively in some contexts because it refers to cohorts that progress to a specific disorder [N1-F1]. This category is also tied to function and risk, because it often includes symptoms that impair functioning and are used to identify individuals who may later develop a disorder [N1-F1; N5-F2].

The biomarker/diagnostic category emphasizes objective or measurable evidence of disease biology that precedes formal diagnosis. This is especially prominent in Alzheimer’s and related dementias. The N3 evidence shows that research diagnostic criteria for Alzheimer’s disease rely on biomarkers such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau, and that the preclinical/prodromal stage is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The same N3 evidence also notes that the lack of a well-established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms and intervention, which suggests that biomarker-based definitions are still under development and sometimes ambiguous [N3-R2]. In dementia with Lewy bodies, the prodromal phase is defined in part by mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features, which reflects a blend of clinical and biomarker criteria [N3-R4]. This category emphasizes validation through biomarker evidence rather than purely subjective symptoms [N3-F3].

The methodological/operational category emphasizes how prodrome is defined, measured, and operationalized in studies. The N4 evidence frames operational definitions as descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions, and one N4 source specifically categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. This category is important because it addresses how researchers distinguish prodrome from other pre-onset states and how they apply definitions consistently. The N4 evidence also highlights that operational definitions are a core methodological approach in psychology for relating observed data to theoretical constructs [N4-R3].

Across fields, these categories overlap and conflict. In psychiatry, prodrome is often a clinical/prognostic concept tied to early symptoms and relapse, but it also needs operationalization to be used in research and diagnosis [N1-F1; N5-F2]. In neuroscience and dementia research, prodrome is increasingly defined by biomarkers and preclinical stages, which can conflict with purely clinical symptom-based definitions [N3-R1; N3-R3]. The overlap is especially visible in schizophrenia prodrome, where prodrome is described as a heterogeneous group of behaviors temporally related to psychosis onset, but the concept itself is an evolving, not a hardbound set of signs [N5-F2]. The conflict arises because different fields may prioritize different criteria: symptoms in psychiatry, biomarkers in neurology and dementia, and operational procedures in research design [N1-F1; N3-F3; N4-R2].

Overall, the main classification schemes are clinical/prognostic, biomarker/diagnostic, and methodological/operational. Each emphasizes different aspects: symptoms and timing in clinical/prognostic, biomarker evidence in diagnostic/prodromal stages, and operational criteria in methodological work [N1-R1; N3-R1; N4-R2]. The categories often overlap, especially between clinical and biomarker-based definitions, and they conflict when different fields use different thresholds or criteria [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2].

## How are prodrome definitions categorized, and what are the main characteristics of each category?

Prodrome definitions are best understood as falling into several overlapping but conceptually distinct categories, each emphasizing different aspects of the phenomenon: symptoms and timing in clinical/prognostic definitions, biomarker evidence and staging in diagnostic/prodromal definitions, and operational procedures in methodological definitions. These categories do not exist in isolation; they overlap in practice, and they often conflict when different fields prioritize different criteria [N1-R1; N1-F1; N3-R2; N3-R4; N4-R2].

### 1. Clinical/prognostic category: early symptoms linked to risk and transition
This category is the most intuitive and historically central. It defines prodrome as the early symptoms and signs of illness that precede characteristic manifestations, and in psychiatry it is also described as the initial prodrome or relapse prodrome [N1-R1]. The evidence emphasizes that prodrome is often used to identify individuals at risk of impending psychosis, and that early intervention may improve long-term outcomes [N5-F2]. In schizophrenia, the prodromal stage is described as consisting of nonspecific symptoms such as lack of motivation, disorganized speech, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms that harm functioning [N5-R1; N5-R3; N5-R4]. The N5 evidence also notes that the prodrome is heterogeneous and is described as a “moment to moment march of psychological changes,” rather than a fixed set of signs [N5-F2].

The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Symptoms**: early, nonspecific, and often functionally impairing [N5-F2].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: a constellation of symptoms occurring before a clear psychotic episode and linked to transition [N5-F2].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through follow-up and outcome data, and historically through DSM-III-R criteria for schizophrenic prodrome, although those criteria were later dropped from DSM-IV [N5-F2; N5-F2].

The clinical/prognostic category is strongest for identifying risk and predicting transition, but it is less robust when definitions are unstable across systems or when symptoms overlap with normal variation [N1-F1; N5-F2]. Its practical challenge is that it can conflate symptoms with risk, and it may be less precise for identifying who will develop a disorder prospectively than for predicting relapse or transition [N1-F1].

### 2. Biomarker/diagnostic category: objective evidence before formal diagnosis
This category is increasingly prominent in dementia and neurodegenerative research. It defines prodrome as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder, and it relies on biomarker evidence such as β-amyloid, total tau, and phosphorylated tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In Alzheimer’s research, the prodromal stage is also linked to preclinical and early disease stages, reflecting a staging model rather than merely a symptom phase [N3-R3]. For dementia with Lewy bodies, the prodromal phase includes mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4]. The N3 evidence also notes that research diagnostic criteria are used to classify participants, and that biomarker evidence is central to participant selection and disease progression analysis [N3-F3].

The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Features**: objective biomarker evidence and preclinical stages, sometimes combined with clinical symptoms [N3-R1; N3-R3; N3-R4].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: combinations of biomarker abnormalities and cognitive impairment, and sometimes formal staging criteria [N3-F3].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through biomarker consistency, disease progression, and trial outcomes; operational criteria are often research-based and may require specific biomarker assessments [N3-F3].

This category is especially strong where biomarker evidence is well established and where trial data link prodromal status to clinical outcomes. However, it faces challenges because biomarker-based definitions may not fully capture clinical symptoms or function, and the evidence notes that the lack of an established, operationalized prodromal definition has limited research into early disease mechanisms [N3-R2; N3-F3].

### 3. Methodological/operational category: how prodrome is defined and measured
This category is less about what the prodrome is, and more about how it is defined, measured, and operationalized in studies. The evidence frames operational categories as descriptions of procedures and criteria used in experimental or observational interventions [N4-R1]. One source specifically categorizes operational definitions for first-episode psychosis into three types: first treatment contact, duration of antipsychotic medication, and other criteria [N4-R2]. The main characteristics of this category are:
- **Features**: procedures, criteria, and study-specific symptom reporting [N4-R1; N4-R2].
- **Thresholds/criteria**: operational criteria such as qualifying prodrome events, baseline reporting, or treatment timing [N2-R1; N2-R3].
- **Validation/operationalization**: through study design and outcome measures, and by providing consistent ways to measure and compare prodrome across studies [N4-R1; N4-R2; N2-R5].

This category is strong for research and study design because it addresses how prodrome is measured and compared across settings. However, it is less robust when operational definitions are too narrow, field-specific, or inconsistent across studies [N4-R2; N4-R3].

### 4. Disease-specific categories and how they differ by disorder
Prodrome definitions vary substantially across disorders because the relevant symptoms, timing, and functions differ.

- **Schizophrenia**: prodrome is a clinical/prognostic concept emphasizing nonspecific early symptoms and risk of psychosis [N5-F2]. The evidence highlights disorganized speech, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms that impair functioning [N5-R1; N5-R3; N5-R4]. It is also noted that the prodrome is heterogeneous and not a hardbound set of signs [N5-F2].
- **Migraine**: prodrome is more operational and symptom-timed. It is defined as the first phase of migraine, with common prodromal symptoms such as sensitivity to light, fatigue, neck pain, and sensitivity to sound [N2-R1; N2-R4]. Treatment during prodrome can reduce headache severity, showing the practical relevance of timing and intervention [N2-R3; N2-R5].
- **Dementia and Alzheimer’s**: prodrome is increasingly biomarker/diagnostic. It is defined as occurring before a clinical diagnosis of cognitive disorder and is linked to biomarker evidence such as β-amyloid and tau [N3-R1; N3-R3]. In Lewy body dementia, prodrome includes mild cognitive impairment, delirium-onset, and psychiatric-onset features [N3-R4].

### 5. Clinical vs research vs diagnostic usage
Prodrome is used differently across contexts:
- **Clinical usage**: strongest in psychiatry, where it is used to identify individuals at risk of psychosis and to guide early intervention [N5-F2].
- **Research usage**: prominent in migraine and dementia research, where prodrome is operationalized through symptoms, biomarker criteria, and study-specific thresholds [N2-R4; N3-F3].
- **Diagnostic usage**: strongest in biomarker-informed dementia research, where prodrome is used as part of research diagnostic criteria and staging [N3-R1; N3-R3; N3-F3].

This distinction matters because the same prodrome concept can be treated as a risk signal, a measurable phase, or a formal diagnostic category depending on the field [N1-F1; N5-F2; N3-R4].

### 6. Common limitations and measurement challenges
Across categories, several limitations recur:
- **Ambiguity in symptom thresholds**: the prodrome is often heterogeneous and not a fixed set of signs, making thresholds hard to apply consistently [N5-F2].
- **Retrospective or operational reliance**: some definitions are retrospective, while others depend on operational criteria, which can be inconsistent across studies [N1-F1; N4-R2].
- **Need for biomarker validation**: biomarker-based definitions require comprehensive assessments, which may be impractical in some settings [N3-F3].
- **Overlap between risk and prodrome**: the distinction between prodrome and risk syndrome is important, because prodrome usually refers to cohorts that progress to a disorder, while risk syndrome may include sub-threshold symptom clusters and other variables [N1-F1].
- **Changing criteria**: in psychiatry, diagnostic criteria for prodrome have changed over time, showing that the category is not stable across systems [N5-F2].

### 7. Field-specific robustness
The robustness of each category varies by field:
- **Clinical/prognostic category**: strongest for identifying risk and transition, but less robust when definitions are unstable or ambiguous [N5-F2; N1-F1].
- **Biomarker/diagnostic category**: strongest where biomarker evidence is well established and linked to progression, but less robust when operational definitions are still evolving or when biomarker access is limited [N3-F3; N3-R2].
- **Methodological/operational category**: strongest for research design and measurement consistency, but less robust when operational thresholds differ across studies [N4-R2; N4-R3].

### Conclusion
Prodrome definitions are best understood as a set of overlapping categories rather than a single fixed concept. The main categories are:
1. **Clinical/prognostic**: early symptoms linked to risk and transition [N1-R1; N5-F2].
2. **Biomarker/diagnostic**: objective biomarker evidence before formal diagnosis [N3-R1; N3-R3].
3. **Methodological/operational**: procedures and criteria for measuring and operationalizing prodrome in studies [N4-R1; N4-R2].

Each category emphasizes different aspects: symptoms and timing for clinical/prognostic, biomarker evidence for diagnostic/prodromal, and operational measurement for methodological definitions. They overlap because prodrome is often studied through multiple lenses, but they also conflict when different fields prioritize different criteria, especially when symptoms, biomarkers, and operational thresholds are not aligned [N1-F1; N3-R2; N5-F2]. Overall, the strongest evidence supports the clinical/prognostic category in psychiatry, the biomarker/diagnostic category in dementia research, and the methodological/operational category in research design [N5-F2; N3-F3; N4-R2].
